Sawaari Mobility: What the Riders Didn't Ask For

Hinjewadi, Pune — 29 September 2026

Ananya Rao, Vice-President of Product at Sawaari Mobility, read the subject line of Robert Kessler's email a second time: "Zaytoon needs the telemetry commitment before Diwali." It was ten in the morning in Pune, which made it half past midnight in New Jersey, and Robert had clearly not slept before sending it. In eight days the roadmap for Sawaari's January release would be locked at the quarterly board meeting, and Ananya had exactly twenty-six person-weeks of engineering capacity to spend on five features that five different people, in five time zones, each considered non-negotiable. She had asked her team to run a Kano survey precisely so that the choice would not be made by whoever shouted last. Now she had the results on her screen, and she still had to decide.

1. A scooter company in a cooling market

Sawaari Mobility was founded in 2019 by two engineers out of IIT Bombay who had worked on battery-management systems at a Pune auto-components supplier. The company builds and sells electric scooters — the Sawaari Uno, its volume model, and the recently launched Sawaari Vega — from an assembly plant in Chakan, with a network of 180 service centres across India. In FY26 it sold just under ninety-eight thousand vehicles and recorded revenue of roughly ₹740 crore, putting it a clear fourth behind Ola Electric, Ather Energy and TVS iQube, and roughly level with Bajaj Chetak and the newer Hero Vida in the sub-₹1.5-lakh segment. The FAME-II subsidy that had propelled the category's first boom wound down in 2024; the government's Production-Linked Incentive scheme for advanced battery cells was reshaping who could compete on cost; and after the 2022–23 spate of EV fires, ARAI's tightened battery-management-system certification had absorbed much of Sawaari's senior firmware team through most of 2026. Differentiation, not subsidy, was now the game, and Ananya's product organisation was the unit expected to find it — inside a materially smaller engineering budget than the company had enjoyed two years earlier.

2. A noisy backlog and a global team

The immediate trigger was commercial. Robert Kessler, Sawaari's VP of Global Sales working out of New Jersey, had spent four months courting Zaytoon Logistics, a Dubai-based last-mile delivery operator, toward a three-year contract: two thousand Sawaari Vega units for its fleet, plus a telemetry-and-service subscription, worth about ₹34 crore in total — roughly a tenth of Sawaari's annual revenue in a single account. Zaytoon's fleet director, Fahad Al Zaabi, had made one condition explicit: every scooter needed live GPS telemetry and remote immobilisation, both to satisfy his own insurers and to meet Dubai's commercial-fleet tracking norms. Robert wanted that feature greenlit immediately, and had suggested the team simply score the whole backlog on reach, impact, confidence and effort and rank it — a method he had seen work at a previous employer. Ananya pushed back: a reach-and-impact score could not tell her whether a feature's absence would sink a rider's rating, or whether its presence would barely be noticed. She asked Divya Menon, Sawaari's data scientist in Toronto, to run a proper Kano study instead — paired functional and dysfunctional questions — across 850 beta riders of the Sawaari Connect app and, separately, 40 fleet-pilot customers, to classify five candidate features by how their presence or absence would actually be felt.

The results, sitting in Exhibit 1, complicated rather than simplified matters. A theft-geofencing alarm that Mei-Ling Tan, Customer Success Lead in Singapore, had been fielding complaints about for months turned out to be a must-be feature for retail riders — invisible when present, but the single most common driver of one-star reviews when absent. Fleet telemetry, the feature Zaytoon needed, was a must-be only for the forty-strong fleet segment; the 850 retail riders were overwhelmingly indifferent to it. Cruise control and an eco/range toggle scored as classic performance features — the more range a rider got, the happier they were, roughly linearly. Voice-assistant integration, which Lena Fischer, Sawaari's design lead in Berlin, wanted for the brand story ahead of the Auto Expo, scored strongly attractive. Ambient LED lighting themes, which Lena also championed, landed mostly in indifferent. Karthik Subramaniam, Head of Engineering in Bengaluru, took one look at the person-week estimates in Exhibit 2 and told Ananya flatly that building all five was not physically possible before the code freeze.

3. The people around the table

Karthik Subramaniam — Head of Engineering, Bengaluru
Controls the twenty-six person-weeks of capacity remaining before the 26 January code freeze, after senior firmware engineers spent most of the year on BMS safety remediation. Wants must-be gaps closed first, on the ground that unresolved must-be defects generate support cost and churn regardless of what else ships.
Lena Fischer — Design Lead, Berlin
Believes Sawaari's retail brand is losing ground to Ather's design language and needs a visible, talked-about feature before the Auto Expo press cycle. Argues that shipping only "invisible" fixes wastes the one marketing moment the January release will get.
Mei-Ling Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Handles both Indian retail escalations and the Dubai account, and is the one person seeing both queues. Reports that theft-related complaints are the top driver of negative reviews, and that Zaytoon has already escalated the telemetry timeline twice.
Robert Kessler — VP Global Sales, New Jersey
Needs the telemetry commitment in writing to close Zaytoon before Diwali, and knows Ola Electric is separately bidding for Gulf fleet accounts. Views the ₹34-crore contract as the clearest revenue Sawaari can bank this quarter.

5. Ananya's options

Option A — Fund the Dubai deal. Build fleet telemetry and immobilisation (22 person-weeks) plus the geofencing alarm (6 person-weeks), using all 26 available weeks. This closes Zaytoon on schedule, banks ₹34 crore over three years, and fixes retail's loudest must-be complaint. Its cost is that cruise control, voice assistant and lighting all slip a full cycle; Lena warns the Auto Expo release will look, in her words, "like a bug-fix update," with no attractive feature to talk about against Ather's newer launches.

Option B — Fund the retail roadmap. Build the geofencing alarm (6 weeks) and cruise/eco mode (8 weeks), leaving 12 weeks free for a scoped-down voice-assistant pilot, and ask Robert to renegotiate Zaytoon's telemetry milestone to the following quarter. This protects retail satisfaction and gives Lena something to show at the Auto Expo, but risks the Dubai contract: Robert is confident Ola Electric would use any delay to reopen the bid, and a lost ₹34-crore account would be visible at board level in a quarter when growth is already slow.

Option C — Split and scope down. Fund both must-be items — the alarm (6 weeks) and a reduced-scope telemetry build covering an initial 500 Zaytoon units rather than the full fleet (roughly 14 weeks instead of 22) — and use the remaining capacity for cruise/eco mode, deferring voice assistant and lighting entirely. Ananya would ask Robert to convert Zaytoon's order into a 500-unit pilot with the balance phased into the following two quarters. This keeps both relationships alive and stays within capacity, but it delivers nothing at full scale: the Dubai pilot may read as under-delivery to Fahad Al Zaabi, and Lena still has no attractive feature to launch.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which of the five features are true must-be features, and why does a must-be classification change how urgently a feature should be funded compared with a performance or attractive one?
  2. Why did the fleet-telemetry feature classify as must-be for the forty-strong pilot segment but indifferent for the 850 retail riders — and what does that imply about running one Kano survey across two different customer segments?
  3. If Ananya had used Robert's reach-times-impact ranking instead of the Kano survey, which features would likely have been ranked highest, and would that ranking have protected Sawaari from the retail one-star reviews Mei-Ling is already seeing?
  4. Which of the three options would you choose, and what would you tell Lena Fischer about why an attractive feature is not funded this cycle?

7. A note for the learner

The Kano model earns its place in this decision because it separates two questions that a plain priority score collapses into one: how much a feature is wanted, and how its presence or absence is actually felt. A reach-and-impact ranking would have treated the geofencing alarm, cruise control and voice assistant as roughly comparable "nice improvements," because all three tested as popular. Exhibit 1 shows that treatment would have been wrong. The alarm is a must-be: riders do not reward Sawaari for having it, but they punish it hard — in reviews, in service-centre visits, in churn — for not having it. Voice assistant is attractive: its absence costs almost nothing, but its presence, done well, is what riders and reviewers talk about. Cruise control sits in between, rewarding investment roughly in proportion to how well it is built. Treating all three the same, as a single backlog score does, risks starving the must-be item that is already costing Sawaari its star rating while overbuilding a feature nobody would have missed.

A well-reasoned answer starts from that asymmetry and then respects the case's second complication: the same feature can be must-be for one segment and indifferent for another, which is exactly what the telemetry row shows. That is not a contradiction to resolve by averaging; it is a signal that retail and fleet are effectively two products sharing a chassis, and that a single 26-person-week budget has to serve two different must-be thresholds, not one.

On that basis, Option C is the most defensible path, not because it is the safest politically but because it is the only option that funds both true must-be features — the retail alarm and a right-sized fleet telemetry commitment — before spending a single person-week on a performance or attractive item. Ananya should tell Karthik that scope, not ambition, is what closes the capacity gap: a 500-unit phased telemetry rollout satisfies Zaytoon's must-be requirement for its first tranche without claiming 22 weeks the team does not have. She should tell Robert that a phased contract, sold honestly as a pilot-to-scale plan, is more defensible with Fahad Al Zaabi than a full commitment Sawaari cannot keep. And she should tell Lena, directly, that an attractive feature funded before a must-be gap is closed is a feature built on top of a leaking roof — voice assistant and lighting are not being rejected, only sequenced correctly, and belong at the top of the next cycle's backlog once the must-be debt is paid down. That is what the Kano lens is for: not choosing the most popular features, but choosing which kind of disappointment or delight is currently at stake, and funding the disappointment first.

The Kano Model: which features are expected, which delight, and which nobody cares about

A working guide to must-be, performance, attractive and indifferent quality — and to the survey that separates them.

1. Bengaluru, 14 January 2026

Ananya Iyer had nine items on a whiteboard and room in the March release for three. She was Vice-President of Product at Gaurika Money, a six-year-old consumer money app in Bengaluru with 2.4 million monthly active users, most of whom used it to pay with UPI, keep a small balance, and occasionally buy a mutual fund. The engineering group had capacity for roughly 340 developer-days in the quarter. The nine items on the whiteboard added up to about 1,100.

The list was a fair sample of how backlogs actually look. Two items came from the customer-support queue: instant re-credit of a failed UPI transaction, and a human on chat within five minutes. Two came from the growth team: a gold round-up feature that swept spare change into digital gold, and a referral leaderboard. Two came from the CEO, who had spent a weekend with a competitor's app: a spend-insights dashboard and a dark mode. One came from the compliance team. Two came from a customer advisory board of eighteen users who, Ananya suspected, were not remotely representative of the other 2.4 million.

The obvious move was to score everything on value and effort and take the top three. Ananya had done exactly that the previous quarter and it had gone badly. The team had shipped a redesigned portfolio screen that scored highest on every axis the group could name, and the number that moved was not retention but the support ticket count, which rose 22 per cent because a fund-switch flow had been buried two taps deeper. Nobody had written down that the fund-switch flow was something users expected rather than something they wanted. That distinction — between what is expected and what is wanted — is the entire content of the Kano model, and it is what Ananya reached for next.

The stakes were specific. Gaurika Money's monthly churn sat at 3.1 per cent, and the board had asked for 2.4 per cent by September. At 2.4 million users, each tenth of a percentage point was roughly 2,400 households a month. Ananya's fear was not that she would pick a bad feature. It was that she would pick three features that were all pleasant and none that were load-bearing, and discover in July that the churn had not moved at all.

2. The idea, precisely stated

The Kano model is a claim about the shape of the relationship between how well a product does something and how satisfied a customer is. The ordinary assumption — the one built into every value-versus-effort grid — is that this relationship is a straight line: more of a good thing produces proportionally more satisfaction. The Kano model says that for most product attributes the line is not straight, and that attributes fall into distinct families depending on how they bend.

The model is named for Noriaki Kano, a quality engineer at what is now the Tokyo University of Science, who presented the idea in 1979 and published it with three colleagues in 1984 in the Journal of the Japanese Society for Quality Control, under the title "Attractive Quality and Must-Be Quality". Kano was working in the tradition of Japanese quality management, where "quality" had come to mean conformance to specification, and he was troubled by an anomaly that conformance could not explain: some improvements delighted customers out of all proportion to their size, while others, done perfectly, produced no detectable gratitude at all. His answer was that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not opposite ends of one scale. The intellectual ancestor is Frederick Herzberg's two-factor theory of workplace motivation from 1959, which had argued the same asymmetry about jobs: the absence of a grievance is not the presence of a motivation.

Kano's families are five. Must-be attributes (also called basic or threshold) cause severe dissatisfaction when absent and produce no satisfaction when present — a bank app that shows your balance correctly earns nothing; one that shows it wrongly loses the customer. Performance attributes (one-dimensional, or linear) behave the way the naive model assumes: more is better, less is worse, roughly proportionally — delivery speed, interest rate, battery life. Attractive attributes (delighters) produce disproportionate satisfaction when present and no dissatisfaction when absent, because the customer never expected them. Indifferent attributes move satisfaction in neither direction; the customer genuinely does not care. Reverse attributes make satisfaction go down when you add more of them — an onboarding tour, a notification, a third confirmation screen.

The one sentence Ananya could say in a steering meeting without sounding glib: "Some of these features earn us credit, some only avoid losing it, and some do neither — and we are currently ranking them as if they all did the same thing." That sentence is the whole model. Everything that follows is the machinery for finding out which is which.

3. How the survey actually works

Kano's method is a paired question. For each attribute, the respondent is asked twice: once in the functional form ("How would you feel if the app re-credited a failed UPI payment within thirty minutes?") and once in the dysfunctional form ("How would you feel if the app did not re-credit it within thirty minutes?"). Both questions offer the same five answers: I like it that way; I expect it to be that way; I am neutral; I can live with it that way; I dislike it that way.

The insight is that the pair of answers, not either answer alone, carries the information. Someone who says "I like it" to the functional question and "I dislike it" to the dysfunctional question is describing a performance attribute — they notice it in both directions. Someone who says "I expect it" and "I dislike it" is describing a must-be — they take it for granted and resent its absence. Someone who says "I like it" and "I am neutral" is describing something attractive. Each of the twenty-five possible combinations maps to a category through a fixed grid, published by Kano and used essentially unchanged since.

A = attractive, O = one-dimensional (performance), M = must-be, I = indifferent, R = reverse, Q = questionable. "Questionable" marks an answer pair that contradicts itself — liking both the presence and the absence of something — and usually means the respondent misread the question or the question was badly worded.

Three steps in this procedure are routinely left implicit, and all three matter. First, the wording of the attribute is itself a decision. "Instant re-credit" and "re-credit within thirty minutes" are different attributes and will classify differently; the level you write into the question is the level you are testing. Second, Q and R responses must be counted, not silently dropped. A Q rate above about five per cent is a signal that the question is broken. A meaningful R rate means a real segment of customers actively does not want the thing. Third, the category is assigned per respondent and then aggregated, usually by taking the most frequent category — the mode. The mode is a crude summary, and Kano practitioners since Berger and colleagues in 1993 have supplemented it with a measure of how decisive the mode is.

4. Gaurika Money's survey, worked line by line

Ananya's team fielded the paired questions to 412 users drawn at random from the ninety-day-active base in early January. Below are the raw counts for four of the nine items. The arithmetic that follows is done exactly as her analyst did it.

Exhibit 2 · Raw category counts, n = 412 respondents per item

Start with the failed-payment re-credit. Discard the R and Q responses, since neither describes a coherent preference for the attribute as written: 412 − 6 − 9 = 397 valid responses. Must-be takes 236 of those, or 236 ÷ 397 = 59.4 per cent. Performance takes 92 ÷ 397 = 23.2 per cent, indifferent 38 ÷ 397 = 9.6 per cent, attractive 31 ÷ 397 = 7.8 per cent. The mode is must-be, and the category strength — the gap between the winning category and the runner-up — is 59.4 − 23.2 = 36.2 points. That is a decisive result. When the gap is under about ten points the mode is not a finding, it is a coin toss.

Two coefficients, introduced by Mike Timko in 1993, convert the same counts into a pair of numbers that can be plotted. The satisfaction coefficient (CS+) is (A + O) ÷ (A + O + M + I): the share of respondents for whom having the attribute adds something. The dissatisfaction coefficient (DS−) is −(O + M) ÷ (A + O + M + I): the share for whom lacking it takes something away, written as a negative number so the two can be plotted on opposite axes. For the re-credit: CS+ = (31 + 92) ÷ 397 = 123 ÷ 397 = 0.31, and DS− = −(92 + 236) ÷ 397 = −328 ÷ 397 = −0.83.

Read those two numbers together. A CS+ of 0.31 says that shipping instant re-credit will delight less than a third of users. A DS− of −0.83 says that not shipping it will actively annoy more than four in five. This is the signature of a must-be, and it explains why must-be features are chronically under-built: every instrument that measures upside rates them poorly.

Running the same arithmetic across the other three items: five-minute human support gives 396 valid, CS+ = (46 + 171) ÷ 396 = 0.55 and DS− = −(171 + 121) ÷ 396 = −0.74, with performance as the mode at 43.2 per cent — it earns credit and costs credit, the classic one-dimensional shape. The gold round-up gives 391 valid, CS+ = (188 + 61) ÷ 391 = 249 ÷ 391 = 0.64 and DS− = −(61 + 22) ÷ 391 = −83 ÷ 391 = −0.21, with attractive as the mode at 48.1 per cent: high upside, almost no downside. Spend insights gives 398 valid, CS+ = 170 ÷ 398 = 0.43 and DS− = −154 ÷ 398 = −0.39, with indifferent as the mode at 42.7 per cent — the CEO's favourite item was the one the largest single group of users did not care about either way.

The second pass: what changes when one input changes

Ananya's analyst then re-ran the gold round-up figures by segment rather than in aggregate, which is the single most informative thing anyone does with a Kano dataset. Among the 148 respondents aged 22 to 28 with self-reported monthly income under ₹40,000, the split was A 93, O 21, I 24, M 6, R 4 — valid 144, attractive share 93 ÷ 144 = 64.6 per cent, CS+ = (93 + 21) ÷ 144 = 0.79. Among the 121 respondents who had been on the app more than eighteen months and reported income above ₹1.2 lakh a month, the split was A 39, O 13, I 55, M 6, R 8 — valid 113, indifferent share 55 ÷ 113 = 48.7 per cent, attractive 39 ÷ 113 = 34.5 per cent, CS+ = (39 + 13) ÷ 113 = 0.46.

The aggregate figure of 48.1 per cent attractive was not a description of any real user. It was the average of a group that loved the feature and a group that shrugged at it. Nothing about the method warned Ananya of this; only the decision to cut the data did. Had she cut the failed-payment re-credit the same way, she would have found the opposite: must-be at 57 per cent in one segment and 62 per cent in the other — a genuinely universal expectation. Must-be attributes tend to be uniform across segments, which is a useful sanity check: a "must-be" that appears in only one segment is usually a performance attribute in disguise.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Categories belong to attributes at a level, not to features

"Customer support" has no Kano category. "A human agent on chat within five minutes" does, and "a human agent on chat within four hours" has a different one — almost certainly must-be at the four-hour level and performance at five minutes. Practitioners who classify features rather than specified levels of attributes get results that cannot be acted on, because the finding does not tell them how much to build.

Categories decay over time, and the direction is one-way

Kano himself observed the lifecycle: today's attractive attribute becomes tomorrow's performance attribute and next year's must-be. UPI itself is the Indian example everyone recognises — genuinely delightful in 2017, competitively differentiating by 2019, and an absolute expectation by 2022, such that an app without it is now unusable. Nothing travels the other way. This means a Kano study has a shelf life, typically twelve to twenty-four months in consumer software, and that a delighter is a wasting asset: you are buying a period of advantage, not a permanent one.

Indifferent is the most abused category

A large indifferent share can mean three very different things: the attribute genuinely does not matter; the attribute matters only to a segment that is a minority of the sample; or the question was written in language the respondent did not understand. The last is common when product teams write survey items in internal vocabulary. Before killing a feature on an indifferent verdict, check the Q rate and check the segments.

Must-be is a threshold, not a slope

Because must-be attributes flatten once satisfied, investment beyond the threshold buys nothing. A bank app that settles failed payments in thirty seconds rather than thirty minutes is not thirty times better loved. Teams that do not internalise this over-engineer their hygiene and under-fund everything else — and the over-engineering is invisible in any dashboard, because it produces no measurable harm, only a missing opportunity.

The model measures stated preference, with everything that implies

Respondents are predicting their own feelings about a described attribute they have not used. They are systematically bad at this, particularly for anything novel, and particularly when the description is flattering. Kano data is strong evidence about must-be attributes, where people know exactly what they expect, and much weaker evidence about attractive ones, where the honest answer to "how would you feel?" is often "I have no idea until I try it."

It says nothing about cost, and nothing about business value

A Kano study will happily tell you that an attribute is attractive to 70 per cent of users when the attribute would take two years and a banking licence to build. It also does not know which customers are profitable. A must-be for a segment that generates 2 per cent of revenue is not automatically more urgent than a delighter for the segment that generates 60 per cent. Kano is an input into prioritisation, not a prioritisation method.

Sample sizes are smaller than people think, but not that small

With 400 respondents, the standard error on a category share near 50 per cent is about √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 400) = 0.025, or 2.5 percentage points. Two categories separated by five points are not reliably separated at all. This is why category strength matters more than the mode: a 36-point gap is real; an 8-point gap is noise wearing a label.

The dysfunctional question is where surveys break

Respondents find "how would you feel if it did not do X?" awkward, and rush it. Badly worded negatives produce Q responses and, worse, produce confident-looking M classifications that are artefacts of double negatives. The cheapest safeguard is to read every dysfunctional item aloud; if it takes two attempts to parse, rewrite it.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the respondent and the payer are the same person, the sample is cheap and large, and the lifecycle decay is fast. Gaurika Money can field 400 responses in a week for the cost of a push notification. The risk is that the sample over-represents engaged users, who have systematically different must-be expectations from the dormant majority whose churn you are trying to prevent.

In B2B products the respondent and the payer are usually different people, and this breaks the arithmetic quietly. At Gunjan Fleet Cloud, a Pune company selling telematics software to transport operators, the procurement head and the dispatcher answer the same question with different categories: statutory e-way bill integration is a must-be for the buyer and an indifferent for the driver; a one-tap shift handover is attractive to the dispatcher and invisible to the buyer. Pooling both groups into one sample produces a ranking that describes nobody. The fix is not statistical, it is to run and report the study by role, and to decide explicitly whose satisfaction the release is buying.

In marketplaces the asymmetry is sharper still, because the two sides trade the same attribute in opposite directions. On Godhuli Bazaar, a handloom marketplace, a seven-day no-questions return window is close to a must-be for buyers and close to a reverse attribute for weavers, who bear the cost. A Kano study run on the demand side alone will recommend something that damages supply. Two studies, read side by side, are the minimum.

By stage: an early-stage company usually cannot afford a 400-person survey and does not need one, because its must-be list is short and obvious, and its real question is whether anything it has is attractive at all. Ten well-run paired-question interviews will settle that. A large company has the opposite problem: it has satisfied the must-be list so completely that the whole organisation has forgotten which features are load-bearing, and it is at constant risk of "simplifying" one of them out of the product. At scale, the Kano study's highest-value output is not the delighter list — it is the must-be inventory that tells the redesign team what they are not allowed to touch.

7. Common mistakes

Ranking by satisfaction coefficient alone

Symptom from the outside: the roadmap is full of pleasant features and the support queue is full of the same three complaints quarter after quarter. Underlying misunderstanding: treating CS+ as a measure of importance, when it measures only upside. Cheapest diagnostic: sort the backlog by DS− instead and see whether the top three items have ever been scheduled.

Surveying only the features you already intend to build

Symptom: every Kano study confirms the existing plan. Misunderstanding: that the survey discovers what customers want, when it can only classify the attributes you put in it. Diagnostic: count how many items in the last study came from the support-ticket taxonomy or from cancellation interviews rather than from the roadmap. If the answer is zero, the study is a mirror.

Treating the aggregate mode as a fact

Symptom: a feature classified attractive lands and the usage curve is bimodal or flat. Misunderstanding: that a category applies to the population rather than to a respondent. Diagnostic: compute category strength; if it is under ten points, or if any single segment flips the category, report the segments and not the aggregate.

Running Kano once and citing it for years

Symptom: a two-year-old deck is still quoted to justify not building something. Misunderstanding: that categories are properties of features rather than of a moment in a market. Diagnostic: ask when the study was fielded and what a named competitor shipped since. If a rival has shipped the attribute, its category has already moved.

8. What good looks like

A team that handles this well does four unglamorous things. It writes attribute statements at a specific level, with the number in the sentence. It fields the paired questions to a sample that includes people who have recently left, not only people who are still there. It reports three columns for every item — the mode, the category strength, and the segment in which the category differs — and refuses to report a mode without the other two. And it treats the output as a constraint on prioritisation rather than as the prioritisation: must-be gaps become entry conditions for the release, performance attributes get a target level and a budget, and attractive attributes compete against one another for whatever capacity remains.

The tell is in the language of the planning meeting. In a team that has absorbed Kano, nobody asks "how valuable is this feature?" They ask "what happens if we do this badly, and what happens if we do it brilliantly?" — and they expect the two answers to be different.

9. What Ananya decided

She took the failed-payment re-credit, the five-minute human support target, and the gold round-up — and she cut the spend-insights dashboard, which required her to tell the CEO that the largest group of users was indifferent to his weekend discovery. Her reasoning was structured rather than instinctive. The re-credit went in because a DS− of −0.83 on a universal must-be is the closest thing product management offers to a certain loss avoided; she estimated from the support taxonomy that failed-payment disputes preceded 14 per cent of the previous quarter's cancellations. Support response time went in at a reduced ambition — a ten-minute target rather than five, because performance attributes have a slope and she could buy most of the gain for a third of the staffing. The gold round-up went in because it was the only item with a real delighter profile, and she scoped it to the under-₹40,000 segment where CS+ was 0.79 rather than building it for everyone.

What she did not do was pretend the model had made the decision. Kano told her what kind of thing each item was. The judgement about how much churn a must-be was worth, and whether a delighter for a third of the base justified the engineering, remained hers.

What to learn next: value versus effort, because Kano supplies the value axis with a shape but nothing about cost; and RICE scoring, because once you know a feature is a must-be you still have to argue about reach and confidence with people who have their own numbers. The natural companion behind you is pains and gains — Kano is, in one reading, simply a classification of how pains and gains feel when they are met or missed.

Two questions to sit with. First: in the product you work on, name the three attributes that are pure must-be. When were they last reviewed by anyone, and what would happen to the roadmap if one of them silently degraded? Second: the gold round-up was attractive to 64.6 per cent of one segment and indifferent to 48.7 per cent of another. If you could survey only one of those two segments, which would you choose — and what does your answer reveal about whose product you actually think you are building?

Kano in Command: asymmetric quality, its measurement, and the places it quietly fails

Must-be, performance, attractive and indifferent — the survey that separates them, the arithmetic beneath it, the schools that disagree about what it measures, and what happens at the organisational seams.

1. Two decisions, three months apart

On 18 November 2025, in a converted textile godown in Pune's Bhosari belt that now served as Gulmohar Fresh's head office, Rohan Kelkar was looking at a capacity plan he did not believe. Gulmohar Fresh was a four-year-old quick-commerce grocery business running eleven dark stores across Pune, Nashik and Nagpur, serving about 410,000 ordering households a month at a median delivery time of nineteen minutes. Kelkar, its Chief Product Officer, had roughly ₹18 crore of combined engineering and operations investment to allocate for FY27, and three candidates on the table.

The first was speed: cut the median from nineteen minutes to twelve, which the operations team estimated would require nine additional dark stores at about ₹1.35 crore of fit-out each, plus ₹40 lakh a month of incremental running cost. The second was a no-questions-asked refund on any item the customer marked unsatisfactory, at an estimated leakage of ₹2.6 crore a year. The third was a recipe-led reorder assistant the growth team had been prototyping since August, which would cost about ₹3 crore to build and run, and which the CEO described in board papers as "our delight layer".

Kelkar's difficulty was that the three options were not commensurable. Every framework the company used — a value-versus-effort grid, a RICE sheet — produced a ranking by assuming that customer value was a single quantity that could be more or less of. His instinct, formed over two previous quick-commerce jobs, was that the nineteen-to-twelve-minute investment would buy almost nothing, and that he could not prove it.

Three months later and 900 kilometres south, on 12 February 2026, Devika Raghunathan faced a decision with the same shape and none of the same particulars. She was VP Product at Dhriti Workforce Cloud, a Coimbatore company selling HR and payroll software to mid-market manufacturers — 118 customers, ₹64 crore of annual recurring revenue, about 210,000 employees processed on its payroll engine each month. Gross revenue churn had run at 11 per cent for two years, concentrated among customers in their second renewal.

Raghunathan had two investments competing for the same eleven engineers. One was statutory compliance automation: generating and filing provident fund, employees' state insurance, professional tax and TDS challans, with automated reconciliation against the payroll run. The other was a shop-floor mobile application for attendance and shift-swap requests, which her design team had user-tested to enthusiastic reviews and which her board had begun referring to, in the same vocabulary Gulmohar Fresh's CEO used, as the delight play. Her own survey data said something awkward about both, and the awkwardness turned out to be the most useful thing in the file.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

The Kano model asserts that the relationship between the level at which a product attribute is delivered and the satisfaction a customer feels is, for most attributes, asymmetric and non-linear — and that attributes sort into families by the shape of that non-linearity. Formally: let s be felt satisfaction and x the delivered level of an attribute. The conventional assumption is that ds/dx is a positive constant. Kano's claim is that ds/dx is a function of x, that it differs qualitatively across attributes, and that the sign and magnitude of the effect of an attribute's absence cannot be inferred from the effect of its presence.

The families: must-be (ds/dx large and positive while x is below a threshold, near zero above it — absence is catastrophic, presence is unremarkable); one-dimensional or performance (ds/dx roughly constant and positive across the range); attractive (ds/dx near zero at low x, rising sharply at high x — absence costs nothing because it was not expected); indifferent (ds/dx ≈ 0 everywhere); and reverse (ds/dx negative). A sixth label, questionable, is not a family but a data-quality flag.

Noriaki Kano, then at the Tokyo Institute of Technology's orbit and later Tokyo University of Science, presented the framework in 1979 and published it in 1984 with Nobuhiko Seraku, Fumio Takahashi and Shin-ichi Tsuji in the Journal of the Japanese Society for Quality Control under the title "Attractive Quality and Must-Be Quality". The problem it was invented to solve was specific to the Japanese quality movement of the period: conformance-to-specification had been enormously successful at eliminating defects, and had run into a wall where products with near-zero defect rates were not winning any additional customer affection. Kano's diagnosis was that the quality movement had been optimising a variable — absence of failure — that saturates. The direct intellectual ancestor is Frederick Herzberg's 1959 two-factor theory of job satisfaction, which made the identical structural claim about work: hygiene factors cause dissatisfaction when absent and no satisfaction when present; motivators do the reverse.

Around this core, four schools have grown up, and they disagree in ways that matter at the level of a real decision.

The classical categorical school

Kano himself, and Berger and colleagues in their 1993 Center for Quality Management Journal paper, hold that the category is a discrete property of an attribute at a stated level, for a defined customer segment, at a point in time, and that the paired functional/dysfunctional question measures it. They would sign: "an attribute's category can change with the level tested and with the segment asked, and the survey must therefore specify both." They would not sign: "the categories are arbitrary bins on a continuum" — they regard the discreteness as substantive, because the design implications differ in kind, not in degree.

The coefficient or continuous school

Mike Timko (1993) and, in a European tradition, Kurt Matzler and Hans Hinterhuber (1998) treat the categorical assignment as a lossy compression of a two-dimensional vector: a satisfaction coefficient and a dissatisfaction coefficient, both derivable from the same raw counts. They would sign: "two attributes classified as performance may have completely different design implications, and the mode hides that." They would not sign: "report the mode and stop." Their practical objection is that most real backlogs contain very few clean must-be or clean attractive attributes and a great many ambiguous middles, and that the categorical method throws away precisely the information needed to tell those middles apart.

The revealed-preference or econometric school

This tradition, whose canonical technique is Randall Brandt's penalty-reward contrast analysis (1987) and whose most-cited empirical support is Eugene Anderson and Vikas Mittal's 1997 demonstration that satisfaction-to-retention links are themselves asymmetric, accepts the asymmetry and rejects the instrument. Its adherents would sign: "asymmetric quality is real and is one of the more robust findings in the satisfaction literature." They would not sign: "you can recover the asymmetry by asking people how they would feel about a hypothetical feature." Their method is to regress an overall satisfaction or retention outcome on dummy-coded high and low performance on each attribute, taken from behavioural or transactional data, and to read the asymmetry from the difference between the penalty and reward coefficients. Their charge against survey Kano is that it measures respondents' theories about themselves.

The design-conversation school

A large body of practitioners, particularly in software, hold that Kano's value is as a vocabulary that disciplines argument, and that the survey apparatus is optional theatre. They would sign: "asking 'what happens if we do this badly?' separately from 'what happens if we do this brilliantly?' improves decisions." They would not sign any claim that a category percentage is a measurement with an error bar. The strongest version of this position is not laziness; it is a claim about where the uncertainty actually sits, which we return to in section 10.

3. Mechanics in depth, worked through

The instrument is a pair of questions per attribute: functional ("How would you feel if the service delivered your order within twelve minutes?") and dysfunctional ("How would you feel if it did not?"), each answered on the same five-point scale — like it, expect it, neutral, can live with it, dislike it. The twenty-five cells of the resulting grid map to the six labels. Assignment happens per respondent; aggregation comes after.

Expert practice adds four things the textbook description leaves implicit, and each is where amateur studies die.

First, the attribute must be written at a specified level, and the level is the variable. This is not a detail; it is the single most consequential methodological choice, and Kelkar's team demonstrated it by testing the same attribute at three levels with 680 respondents drawn from Gulmohar Fresh's ordering base in Pune and Nashik.

Second, the marginal reading matters more than the categorical one. Kelkar's actual question was not "what category is twelve-minute delivery?" but "what does moving from nineteen to twelve buy?" The answer is in the CS+ column: 0.724 − 0.696 = 0.028. Shaving seven minutes off the median would increase the share of customers who feel positively affected by roughly 2.8 percentage points. Against ₹12.15 crore of capital expenditure plus ₹4.8 crore of annualised operating cost, that is approximately ₹6 crore of first-year spend per percentage point of CS+. The investment case was never "go faster"; it was "do not get slower", and that is an operations-reliability problem, not a dark-store problem.

Third, expert practice records two aggregate statistics alongside the mode. Category strength is the mode's share minus the runner-up's share — 75.2 − 15.7 = 59.5 points for the twenty-five-minute row, a decisive classification; 52.6 − 22.8 = 29.8 points for the twelve-minute row, also decisive but less so. Total strength, from Berger and colleagues, is (A + O + M) ÷ valid — the share of respondents for whom the attribute registers at all. For twelve-minute delivery that is (341 + 128 + 31) ÷ 648 = 500 ÷ 648 = 77.2 per cent, which tells you that the 22.8 per cent indifferent share is a real minority and not a warning that the question misfired.

Fourth, statistical modesty. With 648 valid responses, the standard error on a proportion near 0.5 is √(0.25 ÷ 648) = 0.0196, about two percentage points. The difference between two independent shares has a standard error of roughly √2 × 0.0196 ≈ 0.028. So a category separated from its runner-up by six points is not separated; a category separated by thirty is. Most Kano decks in circulation report differences of four or five points as findings. At a more typical fielded sample of 150, the standard error rises to √(0.25 ÷ 150) = 0.041, and nothing under about twelve points should be spoken aloud.

Second-order effects experts watch for

The saturation effect: because must-be attributes flatten, a company that already meets the threshold will measure very little satisfaction impact from them and will systematically underfund their maintenance — until the day a regression pushes performance below the threshold and the loss is discontinuous rather than gradual. The migration effect: attributes move down the ladder over time, always in the same direction, as competitors adopt them. The portfolio effect: in a product with many attributes, the must-be set defines a floor that must be cleared before any attractive attribute earns anything at all; a delighter shipped on top of an unmet hygiene factor does not add, it irritates. The priming effect: asking about an attribute makes respondents more conscious of it, which inflates the measured categories of everything in the questionnaire relative to real life. And the selection effect: samples drawn from active users exclude the people who left because a must-be was missing — which is exactly the population whose opinion you most needed.

4. When the model applies, stated as testable claims

Five conditions have to hold before a Kano study means anything. Each can be checked before fielding, and each is applied below to both protagonists.

Claim one: the respondent can imagine the attribute's absence concretely. Test: can they describe an occasion on which they encountered it missing? For Gulmohar Fresh this holds easily — every customer has had a late delivery. For Dhriti Workforce Cloud it holds for the HR head, who has personally paid a late-filing penalty, and fails for the shop-floor employee, who has never thought about PF challan reconciliation and never will.

Claim two: the market has a settled expectation baseline. Kano categories are relative to what the customer has learned to expect, so in a genuinely new category they are unstable. Both protagonists pass: quick commerce has had a settled expectation since roughly 2022, and payroll software since long before.

Claim three: the respondent's satisfaction is causally connected to the business outcome. This is where Raghunathan's case gets interesting. Dhriti Workforce Cloud sells on three-year contracts to a plant HR head; the shop-floor employee's satisfaction affects adoption but not renewal, at least not within a contract term. Gulmohar Fresh has no contract at all, so the customer's satisfaction and the business outcome are almost the same variable, one order removed.

Claim four: attributes are separable. Kano treats each attribute independently, which is false whenever two attributes interact strongly — a faster delivery promise combined with a worse substitution policy can reduce satisfaction even though each attribute measured well alone. Kelkar's twelve-minute option violates this: hitting twelve minutes would have required narrowing the assortment per dark store, which increases substitutions, which the complaint data showed was itself close to a must-be.

Claim five: satisfaction drives retention in this market. Where switching costs are high — integrated payroll systems, regulated data migration — a dissatisfied customer may renew anyway, and Kano's categories will correctly describe feelings that have no financial consequence within the horizon that matters.

The model is actively misleading in four situations. In genuine category creation, where respondents have no baseline and reliably misclassify the novel as indifferent. In regulated domains, where a legally mandated capability is a must-be regardless of what any survey says — asking is a waste of a question. In two-sided markets, where the same attribute has opposite signs on the two sides and any single-sided study recommends self-harm. And where the tested difference is below the perceptual threshold: Kelkar's nineteen-versus-twelve comparison sits close to the boundary at which customers reliably notice a difference in delivery time at all, and a stated-preference instrument will happily report a difference the customer would not detect in use.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product suites

Must-be attributes are inherited across a suite in a way attractive attributes are not. Once Dhriti Workforce Cloud's payroll module files challans automatically, its newly launched contractor-management module is expected to do the same — customers generalise hygiene expectations across a brand far more readily than they generalise delight. The practical consequence is that the must-be list for a new module is not discovered by surveying that module's users; it is largely inherited from the flagship, and can be read off the flagship's support taxonomy on day one.

Two-sided markets

On Ganika Bazaar, a Surat-based marketplace connecting handloom and powerloom units to apparel brands, a seven-day no-questions return window classified as must-be for buyers (M 61 per cent of 244 valid) and as reverse for suppliers (R 38 per cent of 187 valid, with a further 29 per cent must-be in the opposite direction — they required the window to be shorter). No aggregation of these two studies produces a number. The only honest treatment is to hold both studies side by side and make an explicit judgement about which side of the market is scarcer, which in handloom sourcing is almost always supply.

Regulated products

At Gopika Insure Cloud, which builds policy administration software for general insurers, a substantial part of the backlog exists because the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India requires it. These items have no Kano category worth measuring: they are constraints, not choices. The subtle error is the converse one — assuming that because an item is regulatory it is only a constraint. Regulatory capabilities often contain performance attributes hidden inside them: the filing must happen, but how much manual reconciliation the filing costs an insurer's operations team is a genuine performance attribute with a real slope, and that is where the differentiation lives.

Hardware plus software

Physical products invert the usual asymmetry between what customers can articulate and what they care about. Software must-be attributes are usually nameable — it should not crash, it should load. Hardware must-be attributes are frequently unnameable because they are properties customers experience only as failures: calibration drift, cartridge cost per test, connector durability. A feature-list Kano survey will never surface them, because a feature list does not contain them. Section 8's failure case is exactly this.

AI-native products

Three things change. First, the must-be attribute is probabilistic rather than binary: an assistant that is correct 95 per cent of the time is not 95 per cent of a correct assistant, and users' tolerance for error is itself asymmetric and task-dependent. At Grantha AI, a Bengaluru company building contract-review software for corporate legal teams, a paired-question study on "flags every indemnity clause" classified as must-be at 82 per cent; a follow-up that specified "flags every indemnity clause, with about one false positive per contract" classified as performance, and at "three false positives per contract" the mode moved to reverse. The category of an AI capability is a function of its error rate, and studies that do not state an error rate are not testing the product. Second, attractive attributes decay faster than in any other product class: capabilities that delighted in one quarter are table stakes in the next, compressing the migration timeline from years to months. Third, the reverse category is unusually populated — proactive suggestions, unrequested summaries and automatic actions all produce meaningful reverse responses, and teams that do not test dysfunctionally never see it.

The organisational seams

Kano categories differ systematically by where in the company you sit, and mature organisations manage this rather than resolve it. Sales is structurally biased toward attractive attributes, because those are what win a competitive deal. Support is structurally biased toward must-be attributes, because those generate its volume. Finance sees performance attributes, because those have slopes that can be modelled. What large companies say they do is reconcile these into one prioritised list. What they actually do, when they do it well, is run three separate processes: a hygiene process owned by support and engineering with its own protected capacity, a performance-target process owned by the product and finance groups, and a small, deliberately speculative delight portfolio. The single-list reconciliation that appears in planning decks is usually a post-hoc description of three parallel decisions.

6. Ten nuances that separate expert from competent

1. The category belongs to a level, not a feature

The tell: an expert's survey items all contain a number. The obvious reading — that "fast delivery" is attractive — is wrong because it is not a proposition; it cannot be built or not built. Exhibit 1 is the demonstration: one attribute produced three categories.

2. The useful reading is marginal, not categorical

The tell: an expert asks what a change buys, and computes a difference between two levels rather than reading one label. The obvious reading — "twelve-minute delivery is attractive, so build it" — ignores that the company already operates at nineteen and has therefore already harvested 0.696 of the available 0.724.

3. Must-be attributes are measured by their gap, not their presence

The tell: an expert audits must-be attributes against actual delivered performance, not against the roadmap. The question is never "do we have it?" but "how often, in the last ninety days, did we fall below the threshold?" Because satisfaction with a must-be is bounded above, the entire value is in the tail of the distribution, which no average will show.

4. Indifferent is a diagnosis of the question as often as of the attribute

The tell: an expert reads the indifferent share together with total strength and the questionable rate. A 45 per cent indifferent share with a 3 per cent questionable rate is a finding; the same share with a 14 per cent questionable rate means the item was unintelligible. The obvious reading — that customers do not want it — mistakes an instrument failure for a preference.

5. Aggregate modes describe nobody when preferences are bimodal

The tell: an expert reports the category by segment before reporting it in aggregate, and treats a category that is stable across segments as more trustworthy than one that is not. Must-be attributes are normally uniform across segments; an attribute that is must-be only in one segment is usually a performance attribute for a specialised need.

6. The dysfunctional question carries almost all the information

The tell: an expert spends most of the drafting effort on the negative form and reads every item aloud before fielding. The obvious reading treats the two questions as symmetric checks on each other; in practice the functional answers cluster heavily on "like it" and discriminate poorly, while the dysfunctional answers spread across the scale and do the classifying.

7. Reverse responses are signal, not noise

The tell: an expert looks at the reverse column before the mode. A 12 per cent reverse share on an onboarding tour, a notification setting or an AI suggestion means a real constituency is being harmed, and the design answer is a default rather than a removal. Teams that fold R into "invalid" destroy the most actionable finding in the dataset.

8. The sampling frame has to include the departed

The tell: an expert's Kano sample deliberately includes churned customers and lapsed users, usually over-sampled. Surviving customers have, by definition, tolerated every must-be failure the product commits; asking only them produces a systematically flattering hygiene picture. This is survivorship bias in its purest form and it biases in exactly the direction that costs the most.

9. Kano is orthogonal to cost, and cost is where the decision actually lives

The tell: an expert never presents Kano output as a ranked list. The categories go into the prioritisation as structure — must-be gaps become release entry conditions, performance attributes get a target level and a budget, attractive attributes compete for residual capacity — and the ranking within each bucket is done with a cost-aware method. Presenting Kano as a ranking is the most common way a good study produces a bad decision.

10. Stated preference is strong evidence about hygiene and weak evidence about delight

The tell: an expert weights the two halves of the output differently. People know precisely what they expect and are reliable about it; people are poor forecasters of their own reaction to something they have not experienced. The practical rule is to treat must-be findings as near-conclusive and attractive findings as hypotheses to be tested by shipping something small.

7. Differences by product type and stage — and where there are none

In consumer products the respondent is the payer and the user; samples are cheap; migration is fast; and the principal hazard is that the accessible sample is drawn from engaged users while the churn you care about is happening among the disengaged. In B2B and enterprise the buyer and the user are different people with different categories for the same attribute, and the correct treatment is two studies reported separately and weighted by whose satisfaction determines renewal. 8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Example A — Gulmohar Fresh reallocates on the marginal reading

Kelkar's team added a fourth item to the study after mining eleven weeks of complaint transcripts: "if an item you ordered is unavailable, you are told before the order is dispatched and can choose the substitute yourself." It classified must-be at 68.4 per cent of 651 valid responses, CS+ = 0.221, DS− = −0.871. Substitution complaints accounted for 31 per cent of all contacts and preceded 19 per cent of the accounts that stopped ordering within ninety days. The engineering cost was about ₹1.4 crore.

Set that against the twelve-minute option: ₹16.95 crore of first-year cost for +0.028 CS+ on an attribute whose current level already scored −0.789 on dissatisfaction. The comparison is not close, and no value-versus-effort grid would have produced it, because the grid would have scored "faster delivery" as high value on the strength of the attractive classification without ever asking what the marginal move bought.

Example B — Dhriti Workforce Cloud separates buyer and user

After re-cutting the data by role, Raghunathan ran the same treatment on the shop-floor app. Users: A 318, O 121, M 44, I 105, R 9, Q 7; valid 588; attractive share 318 ÷ 588 = 54.1 per cent, CS+ = (318 + 121) ÷ 588 = 439 ÷ 588 = 0.747. Buyers: A 18, O 9, M 6, I 51, R 5, Q 7; valid 84; indifferent 51 ÷ 84 = 60.7 per cent. The shop-floor app was a genuine delighter for a population that does not renew contracts, and an indifferent for the population that does.

That does not make it worthless. Adoption depth is a leading indicator of renewal in workforce software, and an unused system is cancelled at the second renewal regardless of how well it files challans. But the honest framing changed from "delight play" to "a bet that user adoption converts into buyer-visible value within eighteen months, worth roughly ₹4 crore of engineering" — a proposition the board could actually interrogate.

Cloud synchronisation of results classified attractive at 61 per cent; automated quality-control reports classified attractive at 48 per cent; a touchscreen interface classified performance. The company built the top two over fourteen months at a cost of about ₹6.2 crore.

The cost of catching the error late was roughly ₹6.2 crore of misdirected engineering and two years of market position.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and their diagnostics

Attribute lists drawn from the roadmap

Early warning: every study confirms the existing plan. Diagnostic question: how many items in this study came from cancellation interviews, warranty data or the support taxonomy rather than from a planning document? Cost of catching it late: the Dheeman case — a full development cycle spent on the wrong layer of the product.

Pooling incompatible respondent populations

Early warning: a large indifferent share on an attribute the commercial team believes is critical. Diagnostic: re-run the mode within each role and check whether the pooled mode survives. Cost of catching it late: a quarter of investment aimed at the wrong constituency, and, worse, a defensible-looking data trail justifying it.

Surveying only survivors

Early warning: the must-be list is short and everything on it is already satisfied. Diagnostic: what proportion of the sample has churned, lapsed, or downgraded in the last six months? If it is zero, the hygiene picture is fiction. Cost of catching it late: chronic churn that no roadmap addresses because no instrument sees its cause.

Reading the mode without category strength

Early warning: categories that flip between two consecutive studies. Diagnostic: what was the gap between the winning and runner-up categories, and what is the standard error at this sample size? Cost of catching it late: credibility — a team that reports a category reversal it cannot explain loses the right to run the next study.

Treating Kano output as a ranked backlog

Early warning: a prioritisation deck whose order is "all must-be, then all performance, then all attractive". Diagnostic: does any item's position depend on its cost? If not, cost has not entered the decision. Cost of catching it late: a year spent gold-plating hygiene while a competitor takes the differentiated position.

Letting a study age

Early warning: the study is cited more often than it is re-read, and the deck's date is more than eighteen months old. Diagnostic: which attributes has a named competitor shipped since fielding? Every one of those has moved down the ladder. Cost of catching it late: defending a decision not to build something on evidence that expired before the argument started.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the paired question measure anything real?

The revealed-preference school's strongest case is the retest evidence: independent studies have found that a meaningful minority of attributes change category when the wording is varied, when the order of items is changed, or when the same respondents are asked again weeks later. If a measurement moves that much under irrelevant perturbation, the argument runs, it is measuring the instrument. Their alternative — penalty-reward contrast analysis on behavioural data — has no such problem because it never asks a hypothetical question. The counter-case, which is also strong, is that penalty-reward analysis can only measure attributes the product already has at varying levels; it is silent on anything unbuilt, which is most of what a roadmap contains. For the revealed-preference position to be decisive, it would have to be true that the instability is concentrated in attributes that matter; the available evidence suggests it is concentrated in the ambiguous middle, where the categorical answer was never load-bearing.

Discrete categories or continuous coefficients?

The categorical school's case is that the design implications differ in kind: a must-be attribute needs a threshold and a monitoring regime, a performance attribute needs a target and a budget, an attractive attribute needs a bet. Collapsing these into a point on a plane invites teams to treat a strong must-be and a strong performance attribute as interchangeable because their coefficients are similar in magnitude. The continuous school's case is that real backlogs are full of attributes whose modes are decided by four points, and that forcing a category onto those is false precision in the other direction. What would have to be true for the categorical position to be wrong: that most attributes in practice have weak category strength. In consumer software that is frequently the case; in enterprise software, where must-be attributes are numerous and unambiguous, it is frequently not.

Is migration universal?

The lifecycle claim — attractive becomes performance becomes must-be — is treated as settled in most teaching material and is not. It is strongly supported for attributes that competitors can copy. It is much weaker for attributes rooted in brand, taste or craft, where decades pass with no migration, and it does not obviously hold for attributes that depend on a network the copier cannot replicate. The honest position is that migration is a property of imitability, not of time, and that a team should ask how quickly this particular attribute can be copied rather than assuming a universal clock.

Should Kano drive prioritisation at all?

One camp holds that Kano belongs upstream of prioritisation, structuring the backlog into buckets that are then ranked by cost-aware methods. Another holds, more radically, that the categorical output should never leave the room — that its value is entirely in the argument it forces, and that writing "must-be, 73 per cent" in a planning document converts a useful conversation into a spurious datum that will be quoted for two years by people who never saw the questionnaire. The second position is harder to dismiss than it first appears, and the Dheeman case supports it: the 61 per cent attractive figure on cloud sync was quoted in every internal document for fourteen months, and its apparent precision was exactly what prevented anyone from asking what was missing from the list.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied Kano produces a four-colour chart and a ranked list. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They ask two questions about every proposal rather than one — what happens if we do this badly, and what happens if we do this brilliantly — and they expect the answers to be different, which changes the shape of the conversation before any data is collected. They write numbers into attribute statements as a reflex, because they know the level is the variable. They treat must-be attributes as a monitoring problem rather than a build problem, and they maintain a written inventory of them that new joiners read in their first week, because the most expensive failure available to a large product organisation is to simplify away a load-bearing feature nobody remembered was load-bearing. And they hold the attractive half of any study loosely: they use it to generate small, cheap, reversible bets rather than to justify large ones, because they know stated preference about the unfamiliar is the weakest evidence the method produces.

The deepest tell is what they do with a surprising result. A competent practitioner re-runs the analysis. An expert asks what is missing from the attribute list — because the most consequential errors in this method are never in the arithmetic.

12. What each protagonist decided

Kelkar funded the substitution-transparency work at ₹1.4 crore, funded reliability engineering to protect the nineteen-minute median at the tail rather than the average — the target became "95th-percentile delivery under 28 minutes", not "median under 12" — and put ₹3 crore into the recipe assistant as an explicitly reversible bet with a six-month kill criterion. The nine dark stores were deferred. His reasoning, recorded in the FY27 plan, was that the marginal satisfaction available from speed had already been substantially harvested at nineteen minutes, that the dissatisfaction coefficient of −0.789 at the current level meant the real risk was regression rather than stagnation, and that the only genuine delighter in the portfolio deserved funding at a scale where it could actually work or actually fail.

Raghunathan split her eleven engineers seven and four. Seven went to statutory compliance automation, on the reasoning that a buyer-side dissatisfaction coefficient of −0.914 on a capability implicated in seven of thirteen cancellations is the closest thing to a certainty her data contained. Four went to the shop-floor application, reframed to the board not as delight but as an adoption-depth hypothesis with a defined eighteen-month test. She also changed the sampling frame permanently: every subsequent study at Dhriti Workforce Cloud reports buyer and user separately and never pools them, and the frame now includes every customer who has cancelled in the preceding twelve months.

Discussion questions. First: Kelkar's twelve-minute option scored highest on the categorical reading and lowest on the marginal reading. Which of those two readings should a board see, and what does presenting only one of them do to the quality of the board's oversight? Second: Dheeman Devices ran a methodologically sound study that produced a ₹6.2 crore error. If the instrument cannot detect what is missing from its own input, what governance — not analysis — would have caught it, and who should own that governance? Third: Raghunathan's shop-floor app delights people who do not sign the cheque. Under what conditions is it right to build for a population whose satisfaction has no contractual consequence, and how would you know eighteen months from now whether you were right?

13. Going deeper

  1. Pains and gains. The upstream idea: Kano is, read one way, a classification of how pains and gains feel when they are met or missed. Working through pains and gains first gives you the raw attribute list Kano then classifies — and, as the Dheeman case shows, the quality of that list dominates everything downstream.
  2. Value versus effort. The natural next step, because Kano supplies a shape for value and says nothing at all about cost. Doing the two together exposes the standard trap: attributes with identical value scores but completely different cost curves above the must-be threshold.
  3. RICE scoring. Once you know an item's Kano category you still have to argue about reach, impact, confidence and effort with colleagues carrying their own numbers. RICE is where Kano's structure meets a common arithmetic, and where the temptation to double-count impact and category first appears.
  4. Weighted scoring and WSJF. The formal machinery for combining several value dimensions with a cost of delay. Kano categories map naturally onto cost-of-delay reasoning — must-be gaps have steep, near-immediate cost of delay; attractive attributes have shallow, deferrable curves — which makes this the most direct place to operationalise what you have just read.
  5. Buy-a-feature. A budget-constrained elicitation method that forces respondents to trade off rather than rate, which corrects exactly the bias Kano is weakest against: everything sounds desirable when nothing costs anything. Running buy-a-feature after a Kano study is the cheapest available test of whether the attractive findings are real.
  6. User story mapping. Supplies the structure that prevents the Dheeman failure: a map of the whole user journey, including the physical and operational steps, from which an attribute list can be derived exhaustively rather than from the roadmap.
  7. Prioritising under constraints. Where all of this lands. Kano tells you what kind of thing each item is; constraints — capacity, regulation, contract commitments, cash — determine what can actually be done about it, and the discipline of sequencing under those constraints is the skill the classification exists to serve.

2. How Nuskha got here

Nuskha was founded in Gurugram in 2019 by Rohit Sablok, a former supply-chain manager at a Delhi pharmaceutical distributor, and Devika Iyer, a registered pharmacist from Chennai who had spent nine years running hospital pharmacies. The original product was unglamorous: photograph your prescription, get your month's chronic medication delivered, repeat. By FY26 the company recorded net revenue of ₹960 crore across roughly 1.9 crore orders, a blended gross margin of 21 per cent, a contribution of ₹110 crore before central technology and marketing, and an EBITDA loss of ₹84 crore. It held ₹290 crore of cash and was burning about ₹9 crore a month.

Two decisions from the company's past constrain what Rukmini can do in January. The first is architectural and commercial at once. In 2023, needing revenue that did not depend on Indian discounting, Nuskha signed a five-year platform licence with Falaj Health Assurance, a Dubai third-party administrator that runs pharmacy benefits for insurers across the Emirates. Falaj wanted Nuskha's ordering and prescription-verification stack white-labelled for the UAE. To win the deal, Nuskha's then-CTO committed to a single shared codebase and accepted a feature-parity clause: any consumer-facing capability shipped in the Indian app must be made available in the Falaj build within two quarters, or Nuskha pays a service credit of ₹1.2 crore per quarter of delay. At the time, with eleven engineers and one product, parity was free. In 2026, with seven candidate features and a UAE regulator that treats prescription data differently from the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, parity is a tax on every delight Nuskha might want to ship.

The second decision was the 2024 launch of Refill Autopilot, a UPI AutoPay standing instruction that re-orders a chronic patient's medicines automatically each month. It was the most celebrated launch in the company's history — 4.1 lakh active mandates within a year, and the single reason Chitrak Capital led the ₹310 crore Series C at the valuation it did. The Series C term sheet carries a covenant: contribution margin must not fall below 10 per cent of net revenue for two consecutive quarters, and headcount additions outside fulfilment require investor consent. Nuskha therefore cannot hire its way out of the January capacity problem.

3. The industry

Indian e-pharmacy in 2026 is a market with three different weather systems. The first is the incumbent digital-health layer: Tata 1mg, PharmEasy, Apollo 24|7, Netmeds, Truemeds and MediBuddy, all competing on assortment, discount and the credibility of their pharmacist review. The second is quick commerce, which arrived without warning. When Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and Blinkit began stocking over-the-counter medicines and delivering them in ten to twenty minutes, they did not take much of Nuskha's chronic-refill revenue; they took something more expensive, which was the customer's sense of what a delivery promise means. In 2021 Nuskha's two-hour metro delivery had been a marketing headline. By 2026 a two-hour promise in Bengaluru or Hyderabad is, in the words of one of Priyanka's verbatims, "fine, I suppose."

The third system is regulatory and, unusually for Indian consumer internet, the most consequential. The long-pending e-pharmacy rules under the Drugs and Cosmetics framework remain unsettled; the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and state drug controllers inspect on the basis of existing law, which means a substitution made without a prescriber's or patient's consent is not merely a customer-experience failure but a compliance exposure. The DPDP Act's consent-and-notice obligations now bind health data explicitly. And the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's ABHA identifiers and health-record lockers have moved from pilot to procurement: two state governments have issued tenders for chronic-disease medicine supply in which ABHA linkage is a qualifying criterion rather than a scored one. Nuskha exports to two markets besides India — the Falaj white-label in the UAE, and a small but high-margin NRI shipping business in the United States built by Aditya Ranganathan out of New Jersey — and each has its own answer to what a prescription is.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence matters, because at each step the company believed something that has since become unreliable.

In March 2026 Nuskha's app-store rating fell from 4.3 to 3.8 over nine weeks. The growth team attributed it to a pricing change. In May, Meera Sundaram's support organisation reclassified its ticket taxonomy and discovered that the largest single category was not pricing at all but orders in which a customer received a different manufacturer's version of the same molecule without having approved it. Operations had been substituting to protect fill rates. Devika Iyer had raised it twice in 2025; both times it had been logged as an operations matter, not a product one.

In July, Aditya's US business and the Falaj account both grew faster than plan, and the board asked why the Indian consumer app was not growing at the same rate. Lukas Brenner, design director in Berlin, proposed a two-part answer: a Generic Savings engine that would show every customer the cheapest equivalent to their prescribed brand, and Health Streaks, an adherence-reward mechanic modelled on consumer fitness apps. Somewhere in Toronto, Priyanka was probably still awake and would say, if asked directly, that the honest answer was to re-field the study — six weeks she did not have, for a confidence she was not sure she would get.

The air-conditioning came back on at ten past one. Rukmini typed a heading into the empty slide, read it, deleted it, and sat looking at the cursor.
